articles.title: Tropical Storm Queenie enters PAR — PAGASA
articles.summary: Tropical Storm Queenie (international name: Surigae) entered the Philippine area of responsibility Thursday morning, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 1:30pm
Satellite rendering shows Tropical Storm Queenie (international name: Surigae) taken as of 10:40 p.m. of Sept. 24, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Storm Queenie (international name: Surigae) entered the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) late Thursday morning, September 24, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.
As of 11 a.m., PAGASA reported that the center of Queenie was estimated at 1,310 kilometers east of Northern Luzon.
The storm was packing maximum sustained winds of 75 kilometers per hour (kph) near the center and gustiness of up to 90 kph, moving west-northwestward at a speed of 35 kph.
No tropical cyclone wind signals had been raised as of posting time.

PAGASA noted that while Queenie is not expected to directly affect land weather conditions over the next three days, its periphery and trough will generate strong to gale-force gusts over Batanes, Babuyan Islands, and Ilocos Norte on Thursday.
From Friday through Saturday, gusty conditions are expected over Davao Oriental, Davao Occidental, and Sarangani.
Cloudy skies with scattered rain showers and thunderstorms are forecast over Batanes and Babuyan Islands starting Saturday, September 26.

Weather forecasters advised mariners operating motor bancas and small sea vessels in Northern Luzon to take precautions or avoid venturing out, as coastal waters will experience slight to moderate seas measuring 1 to 2 meters.

According to PAGASA's track and intensity outlook, Queenie will maintain its west-northwestward trajectory until Friday before curving north-northeastward on Monday, September 28. The storm is expected to exit the PAR by Tuesday morning, September 29.
PAGASA warned that the storm will gradually intensify while inside the PAR and may develop into a typhoon by Sunday, September 27.

articles.title: Judge orders Trump White House to restore access to CNN, MS Now and Politico
articles.summary:
US district judge orders temporary lifting of Trump’s ban on the three media outlets, saying it was likely unconstitutional

A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to restore…

blocks.text: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to temporarily restore ⁠White House ⁠access ​to journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico, ⁠saying his ban on the three media outlets was ⁠likely unconstitutional.
US district judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed ‌contesting the ban that the president announced ​on 18 September.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and issued a temporary restraining order that will be in effect for 14 days. Such orders are typically designed to preserve the status quo pending a closer review of the case by the court.
Earlier on Wednesday Kelly cited past case law that clearly laid out the need for a distinct process that involved advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case.

The judge said that prior cases made clear that “before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard”.

A Justice Department lawyer told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the ​press passes in letters sent to the news outlets ​on Tuesday. But the judge signalled skepticism of that argument, ​noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be ⁠able to constantly write or ​report ​FICTION and LIES,” ​and justice department lawyers ​had ‌sought to ​justify ​the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They requested a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out.

In a legal filing on Tuesday, the ​Justice Department argued that access to the ‌White House is a ​privilege, not an entitlement, and that the ​president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations.

A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organizations filed a legal brief on Wednesday supporting the three news outlets. They asserted that “stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of supreme court jurisprudence.“
The brief was signed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.
With Reuters and the Associated Press

articles.title: Israel facing water shortages caused by destruction of Gaza’s treatment plants
articles.summary:
Five desalination plants shut down for days, while Gaza remains in grip of severe water and sanitation crisis

Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom…
articles.byline: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerualem and Seham Tantesh in Gaza

blocks.text: Israel is facing weeks of water shortages after an exceptional algae bloom crippled much of its desalination capacity, in a crisis scientists say was triggered when Israeli attacks destroyed much of Gaza’s wastewater infrastructure, causing a massive discharge of untreated sewage.

“Pollution does not recognise political borders,” said the Zalul Environmental Association, an Israeli NGO dedicated to protecting the country’s seas and shores. “The discharge of untreated sewage from the Gaza Strip into the sea is contributing to the worsening crisis affecting the Israeli desalination facilities. The wastewater contains nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, which feed microalgae and cyanobacteria and may intensify their blooms.”

Despite last year’s US-brokered ceasefire, Gaza remains gripped by a severe water and sanitation crisis. The Palestinian territory is plagued by rodents, and sewage floods its coastline after Israel destroyed its wastewater treatment plants.

Just across the border, a vast bloom of microalgae stretching up to 60 miles (100km) long has clogged filters at five of Israel’s six main desalination plants, which were shut down for days and have since been operating at a reduced level.

blocks.caption: A satellite view shows an algae bloom along Gaza’s coast to Ashdod in Israel. Photograph: Sentinal Hub/Copernicus.eu

blocks.text: Experts say that after nearly three years of war, the environmental consequences of the destruction in Gaza are now spilling back into Israel.

“The discharge of untreated sewage from Gaza into the sea increases risks to Israel’s water production infrastructure along the southern Mediterranean coast,” said Jack Gilron, a professor emeritus and desalination expert at Ben-Gurion University’s Zuckerberg Institute for Water Research. “The current incident reinforces the need to prepare against threats to one of Israel’s main sources of drinking water.”

Since 7 October 2023, Israeli bombardment has destroyed 90% of Gaza’s water and sanitation infrastructure, according to a report by Médecins Sans Frontières. Direct strikes have been carried out on wells, carrier lines, reservoirs and desalination units.

Gaza’s water crisis remains severe. Before the war, 80% the territory’s supply came from an aquifer under the coastal strip, but that supply is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater and unfit for human consumption.

Most of Gaza’s drinking water came from desalination plants and three pipelines controlled by the Israeli water authority, but those pipelines were cut at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

blocks.caption: In Gaza City, a reservoir has become a sewage collection pool after the destruction of local wastewater infrastructure and pumping stations. Photograph: Faiz Qreqa/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Meanwhile, damaged or destroyed distribution networks have left much of the population reliant on water trucks.
For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease, with acute diarrhoea among the leading causes of illness.

“We carry water in jerry cans,” said Nas al-Barawi, 34, a mother of five from Beit Lahia. “We walk with heavy containers or wait for hours in queues. Much of the water is unsafe, and children suffer recurring stomach infections, diarrhoea and skin rashes. Damaged sewage networks and failed pumps have also left wastewater flowing between tents and through residential areas.”

Omar Shatat, the deputy executive director of the Coastal Municipalities Water Utility in Gaza, said all five of the territory’s wastewater treatment plants were out of service, leaving an estimated 45,000 cubic metres of untreated sewage to flow into the Mediterranean every day.
In addition, about 15,000 cubic metres of untreated waste a day seeps into the groundwater from soakaway pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.

“This is a catastrophic situation environmentally and from a public-health perspective,” Shatat said. “The sea is heavily polluted, and the first people affected are Gaza’s residents and displaced people because they are in direct contact with the highest concentrations of sewage.”

blocks.caption: A man crosses effluent water that runs from the camps housing displaced families in Gaza City towards the Mediterranean. Photograph: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Pat Griffiths, the International Committee of the Red Cross’s spokesperson in Gaza City, said the situation was only likely to get worse with the onset of winter. “Palestinians live surrounded by wastewater. It’s all around them. It’s where they eat, where they get water, where they walk,” he said.

Shaimaa al-Katari, 37, who has been displaced to al-Mawasi, said: “We have nowhere to dispose of the water from washing dishes and clothes. We have to let it run into the street, which causes pools of stagnant water to form. Algae and mosquitoes then spread around them and the streets become dirty. We suffer from foul smells, mosquitoes at night and flies during the day, as well as rodents.”
Rats have infested parts of Gaza for months, thriving amid raw sewage and piles of rubbish accumulating around overcrowded camps for displaced people.

blocks.caption: The Bureij refugee camp in Gaza is fumigated against rodents and insects as infectious diseases increase. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Israeli communities near the Gaza border have also been grappling with an unprecedented rat infestation, with rodents swarming homes and gardens.

“The consequences [of the war] do not stop at the border,” said Nada Majdalani, the Palestine director of EcoPeace Middle East, an environmental peacebuilding organisation. “We are already seeing an increase in hepatitis A in Gaza. I believe we are on the verge of a catastrophe. And a serious outbreak in Gaza would not necessarily remain within Gaza’s borders.”

In Israel, authorities are urging people to use water “judiciously” until the system is fully restored. Water supplies have been reduced in the south of the country, and farmers have been instructed to halt irrigation, which economists say will cause food prices to rise.
Zalul and EcoPeace urged Cogat, the Israeli agency charged with administration of Gaza, to help restore the territory’s sewage system and allow wastewater to be treated in Israeli-controlled areas.
Cogat did not respond to a request for comment.

Zalul said: “If the pollution continues, its impact could eventually be felt throughout the country. When the marine environment is contaminated, both people and nature suffer. Regardless of which side of the border they are on.”

articles.title: OpenAI agent hacked Australia government portal: PM Albanese
articles.summary: The hack of Australian health data marks the world's first known breach of an AI-led breach of a government website.

image.caption: OpenAI said it spotted the breach while carrying out an 'extensive review' of its AI toolsImage: Michael Dwyer/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: An OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government health data portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday, in what is the first known instance of an artificial intelligence hack of a government system.

Albanese said the breach occurred in June when an autonomous OpenAI program accessed both "public and non-public" files on the statistics reporting portal of Medicare — Australia's publicly funded universal health insurance scheme.
The available evidence did not indicate a broader network compromise, Albanese said, adding, "Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" over the incident.
OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said in a statement that it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI tools, adding that "our models took actions we did not intend".
Altman had earlier on Wednesday addressed a UN security council meeting, apprising of AI risks the world faces as the technology develops.
More to follow.

articles.title: Are pubs and pups a good mix? Dog owners delight as Victoria looks to follow the UK and Europe’s lead
articles.summary:
‘Pubs have been pet friendly for years’ in other countries, premier says, as Labor moves to overturn ban on dogs in venues

For Steph and her partner Paul, there’s something special about a…

blocks.text: For Steph and her partner Paul, there’s something special about a pub in the British winter.
“It’s really lovely – in wintertime, you go with your dog, there’s a fire, it’s really cozy,” she said.
Now, they may be able to do the same in Melbourne with their cavoodle, Rupert.

On Thursday, the Victorian premier announced that if Labor was re-elected in November, it would amend the state’s food safety laws to overturn the ban on dogs in venues. Currently, dogs are only allowed to dine with their owners outside in limited circumstances in Victoria, with councils largely responsible for enforcing the rules.
“Not being able to go into some pubs with our dog is the difference between us going in or not,” Steph said.
Though the new parents are aware pets in pubs may not be for everyone.

“There is the exception of large dogs that are potentially scary for younger children and I do understand the issue in that space, but certainly for small, fluffy dogs, it’s hard to understand [why not],” Paul said.
“Kids are more disruptive than dogs, to be honest,” Steph added.

blocks.caption: Paws, pints and 3am pubs in Victorian premier’s election promise – video

blocks.text: For, Zeke, whose family owns six King Charles Cavaliers, including one-year-old Daisy, it requires planning ahead,
“I have to check before I go,” he said. “It always has to be outside, in the beer garden, but a lot of pubs are not allowed.”
Carroll said the change shows the government is moving “with the times”.
“All over Europe, pubs have been pet friendly for years – decades, in fact,” he said.
“What’s been shown in Europe is that pubs that are pet friendly and allow dogs benefit everyone – the economy grows, they become more family friendly, and everyone has a great time.”
The government said it will be up to individual venues if they want to permit pets and it will conduct consultation to determine where exactly they will be allowed.
“Publicans decide the music, the menu and the crowd. They should get to decide whether dogs are allowed inside,” it said.
At the Royal Botanic Gardens on Thursday morning, everyone Guardian Australia approached was supportive of the policy.
Phillip currently picks where to dine out based on whether his tibetan terriers, Pebbles and Mickey, can join him.
“They just sit at the table and watch us eat,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
“They are a big part of the family. And I think if people got their dogs under control, it shouldn’t be a problem.”
Kimberley Malcolm is from the lobby group the Australia Hotels Association. The group had been pushing for clearer guidelines around pets, which she said will benefit both publicans and patrons.

“A lot of us don’t have children, so your dog is your child. To be able to bring them to the pub to enjoy all of the things the pub has to offer, is really cool,” she said, accompanied by her French bulldog Mack.
Friends Gemma and Anna were also supportive – though they don’t think it will be enough to change people’s vote.
“If I wasn’t going to vote for Labor, it wouldn’t switch my vote,” Anna said.
Carroll also announced if re-elected, Labor would scrap legislate for venues to have an “automatic right” to stay open until 3am.
“The red tape and the hurdles they have to go through to get to 3am, to be frank, is ridiculous,” he said.
He also committed to reducing the wait time for standard liquor licences from 11 weeks to six, allow staff under 18 to clear tables and consider more underage gigs at pubs and venues.
Earlier in the week, Labor also announced plans to create live music precincts and committed funding to the arts and regional beer tourism and festivals.
It comes off the back of two polls released this month that show Labor’s primary vote has sunk to between 24 and 25%.
Opposition leader Jess Wilson said she didn’t have a problem with seeing pubs open later – or for dogs in pubs – but the announcements would do little to improve consumer confidence.

“Just because you open the pub to 3am doesn’t mean you’re going to see another pint being bought. So we want to make sure that we actually fix our economy here,” she said, noting the Coalition’s plan to reduce tax burden on businesses.

articles.title: No abuse of discretion in new Sara Duterte impeachment threshold rule -- Tongol
articles.summary: There was no abuse of authority when the senator-judges decided to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 12:29pm

There was no abuse of authority when the senator-judges decided to base the two-thirds vote to convict the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."
In an interview with Unang Hirit’s On Record Thursday, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said the senator-judges conducted due diligence before voting.
He said that the impeachment court consulted retired Supreme Court justices, heard oral arguments, and deliberated before issuing its ruling on the voting threshold.
These steps could be relevant to any future claim of grave abuse of discretion because the Senate impeachment court showed that the issue had been subjected to extensive consideration, he added.

"If you look at the actions of the impeachment court, nag-amici curiae, nag-oral arguments, tapos nag-deliberations (they invited amici curiae, they had oral arguments and then deliberations). So, itong mga proseso na ito (these processes) ensure that the impeachment court came up with this decision with due diligence," Tongol said.
"Ibig sabihin noon, it is antithetical to the grave abuse na sasabihin mo doon sa Korte Suprema. So, technically, this decision by the impeachment court is constitutionally bulletproof," he added.
He said the SC may intervene on the issue of voting threshold if the Senate impeachment court committed grave abuse of discretion, .

“There's always a recourse na kapag ikaw ay aggrieved sa isang desisyon ng isang korte, lagi mong ita-try at ita-try na iakyat sa Korte Suprema to avail of your Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari,” he said.
(There's always a recourse when you are aggrieved by a decision of a court, you will always try to go to the Supreme Court to avail of your Rule 65 Petition for Certiorari.)

“At ipapakita mo na may grave abuse of discretion. Ito 'yung judicial power para matingnan kung ang isang body ay may grave abuse of discretion, amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction,” he added.
(And you will show that there is grave abuse of discretion. This is the judicial power to see if there is grave abuse of discretion by a body, amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.)
According to Tongol, the defense earlier said it would proceed with "abundance of caution,” meaning it will not waive its option to question the proceedings before the SC.

Meanwhile, House prosecution panel spokesperson Benjamin Tolosa Jr. said the six senators who did not participate in the proceedings could still pursue legal remedies before the SC if they choose to do so.

“Ang sabi nila diyan, ito ay political question na ang Senado lamang, sitting as impeachment court, ang makakapag-determine at hindi ito dapat panghimasukan ng Supreme Court,” Tolosa told Unang Balita.
(They said that this is a political question that only the Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, can determine and that the Supreme Court should not interfere.)

Asked about Duterte's spokesperson Atty. Paolo Panelo’s claim that the Senate impeachment court had lost its legal and moral authority to continue the trial, Tolosa said, “Everyone's entitled to their own opinion. No matter how wrong that opinion may be.”

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday voted to base the two-thirds vote to convict impeached Vice President Sara Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of "legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings."

The vote on Wednesday, in effect, set aside the ruling on July 6 by presiding officer Senator-judge Francis "Chiz" Escudero, who set the number of votes needed to convict at 16, or two-thirds of all the 24 senators.

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion put forward by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought reconsideration of the July 6 ruling after some senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.—AOL, GMA News

articles.title: NGCP: 5-hour red alert status over Visayas grid on September 24, 2026
articles.summary: Power interruptions may occur from afternoon until evening as red and yellow alert statuses are declared over the Visayas grid due to tight energy supply, the National Grid Corporation of the…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 12:18pm

Power interruptions may occur from afternoon until evening as red and yellow alert statuses are declared over the Visayas grid due to tight energy supply, the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) said on Thursday, September 24.
In an advisory, the red alert status is up from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. The yellow alert status, on the other hand, would be in effect from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m., and 9 p.m. to 10 p.m.
The Visayas grid is currently running with an available capacity of 2,292 megawatts (MW) against a peak demand of 2,495 MW.

The red and yellow alert status declarations are due to the unavailability of several large coal plants in the Visayas: Therma Visayas, Inc. Unit 1, Panay Energy Development Corp. Unit 3, and KEPCO SPC Power Corporation Unit 2.

The grid operator also cited the temporary unavailability of power import from Luzon due to the requested emergency shutdown of Tabango-Kananga 230kV Line 2 by customer to undertake emergency repairs of their defective equipment.
A red alert status is issued when power supply is insufficient to meet consumer demand and the transmission grid’s regulating requirement.
Meanwhile, a yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement.
To address the thinning energy reserves in the Visayas grid, the Department of Energy (DOE) earlier ordered the NGCP to install over 250 megawatts of battery energy storage system.
The DOE is also mulling to tap liquid fuel facilities to help power up the grid. — RSJ,GMA News

articles.title: CICC, Discord scheduled for meeting following ban order
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) and Discord are scheduled for a meeting on Thursday, September 24, 2026, following a ban order against the media sharing and messaging…

blocks.text: Published September 24, 2026 12:08pm

The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) and Discord are scheduled for a meeting on Thursday, September 24, 2026, following a ban order against the media sharing and messaging platform.
In a message to GMA News Online, CICC Executive Director Undersecretary Renato "Aboy" Paraiso confirmed that Discord is currently banned in the country.

On Wednesday night, the CICC clarified that it did not extend the 24-hour period given to Discord to establish Philippine presence "pending direct discussions with the platform and concrete commitments on the CICC's requirements."
"Discord separately reached out to the CICC in a letter to express its willingness to engage with the agency on its existing teen safety measures," the CICC said.
Paraiso told GMA News Online that "we have a meeting with them (Discord) at 12 noon later.”

The CICC on Tuesday gave both Reddit and Discord 24 hours to establish a Philippine presence within 24 hours to enhance collaboration with the government following the shooting at the Banga National High School in South Cotabato.
The agency earlier said it gave extensions to both Discord and Reddit, but issued a clarification that only Reddit was granted an extension.
Discord told the CICC that the newly rolled out Global Teen Experience would ensure that teenagers are placed in age-appropriate places on their platform.

Discord Senior Public Policy Advisor Vasundhara Singh said users who cannot be placed in a specific age group will have to confirm their age through facial age estimation, with biometric data not being stored in Discord.
The shooting in South Cotabato is the third school shooting incident in 2026.
In June, two students opened fire in a high school in Tacloban, killing three others.
Not more than two months later, in August, another student shot and killed a schoolmate in Ateneo de Zamboanga before turning the gun on himself. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: We need an alternative to big tech platforms: Introducing, MUNI
articles.summary: MUNI, an online community space and network, launches on September 16, 2026. It's time for a platform where facts and trusted voices can thrive.

blocks.text: MUNI, an online community space and network, launches on September 16, 2026. It's time for a platform where facts and trusted voices can thrive.
MANILA, Philippines – Anyone with a social media account can see that our online spaces are not like they were.

Instead of seeing your friends’ posts, you see content you never asked for, from accounts you don’t even follow. Around a third of online content posted after chat bots came into the picture may have been written with AI. We dodge disinformation, AI slop, and toxic sludge on our feeds every day.
And so, we built MUNI.

MUNI was founded on the belief that facts and verified information can thrive, but only in a platform that gives it a chance. MUNI is that platform, which launched on September 15, and can be accessed through the websites of various Philippine news outlets. We want to invite other news groups and civic groups to join us on MUNI.

The predecessor of MUNI is Communities, which we at Rappler launched in December 2023. At the time, we were already getting worrisome signs of how internet enshittification and big tech’s opaque algorithms were driving people away from journalism.

Back then, we envisioned an alternative space where we could bring our readers, our supporters, our partners in the civic space, and even other Philippine news organizations. If the huge platforms we had relied on for distribution and connection were no longer helping us, and were even endangering our community, why not build our own?

That’s what Rappler Communities was for the past three years. It became a space, a digital plaza, where we created public chat rooms centered on our news coverage and civic action. It’s built on top of the Matrix protocol, a messaging system that is decentralized, interoperable, and secure, and now used by governments like Germany and France.

Our reporters sent their live updates and photos from their field coverage to the chat rooms, and our readers could ask them questions in real time. Our partners used the chat rooms to tell us what was going on in their sectors or communities. We used the chat rooms for election monitoring and crowdsourcing incidents of corruption to fuel our investigative journalism. Earlier this year, that anti-corruption Communities initiative won gold at the Digital Media Awards Asia-Pacific, under the audience engagement category.
What we’ve seen is promising. Despite our miniscule newsroom budget and limited resources for a large-scale campaign, Rappler Communities has thousands of regular users.

The use of our chat rooms is now part of regular newsroom operations, for breaking news coverage and scheduled interactions between our journalists and curious community members. We’ve even created chat rooms moderated by civil society groups, civic leaders, and government officials, not just journalists. We’re all guided by one principle: create an online space where facts and verified information can thrive, so that real-world change can happen.
The technology may be new, but the ethos is time-tested: People equipped with facts and top-quality information are able to make better decisions and change their situation.

This September, the month of World News Day, we’re going all-in with Communities, and now want to offer it to as many organizations and people as possible. And so, we’ve renamed it MUNI, a Filipino word that means “to reflect.” It is also a word within, “community,” the heart of this initiative.

We want to invite trusted civic groups, communities, and newsrooms all over the world to create chat rooms on MUNI. Because of the Matrix’s decentralized infrastructure, your chat room can exist within your own apps or websites. In our case, MUNI exists as a tab on the Rappler app. It’s also visible on the websites of two other news outlets: Daily Guardian in Iloilo, and SunStar in Cebu, among others.
The more of us are on MUNI, the more viable this space becomes as an alternative to platforms now dominated by AI slop or profit-driven algorithms.

Explore MUNI by downloading the Rapper app, for free, from App Store or Play Store. Tap the Muni tab at the bottom, then join as many chat rooms as you want. If you already have the Rappler app, just open the app and you will be asked to update it. For some users, it may take time for App Store or Play Store to give you the update option since we have just launched this.
If your organization is interested in joining MUNI, please email us at community@rappler.com by October 31, 2026, so we can invite you to an exploratory meeting about MUNI.
Let’s assert our independence from tech platforms that don’t prioritize facts and verified information. Let’s give ourselves, and our community, a real choice. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Australia says OpenAI agent hacked into government website
articles.summary: The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States

blocks.text: OPENAI. A keyboard is placed in front of a displayed OpenAI logo in this illustration taken February 21, 2023.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States

items: An OpenAI agent breached an Australian government health data portal in June, marking a significant incident of AI hacking a government website.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese expressed extreme concern over the breach, noting a delay in notification from OpenAI and the potential impact on other government websites.
OpenAI stated that no patient records were accessed, only aggregate health statistics, and acknowledged unintended actions by their models in accessing several Australian government systems.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

SYDNEY, Australia – Australia said on Wednesday, September 23, an OpenAI agent breached a government health data portal in June, gaining unauthorized access to files, in what could be the first known instance of an AI agent hacking a government website.

The breach is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the United States, coming on top of several recent breaches globally by rogue AIagents that have alarmed governments and companies.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the medical statistics portal of a government agency responsible for non-sensitive health data and statistics, including public medical spending.

“Evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the … network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said during a media briefing in New York, where he is attending the UN General Assembly.

Investigations continue and Australia had voiced its “extreme concern about this incident” to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese said, adding that he was deeply disappointed by the company’s delay in notifying the government.

“It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all,” Albanese said, adding that the investigation would also examine why government systems had failed to detect the breach in the first place.
He also warned that three other government websites “may be impacted” by the OpenAI agent’s activity.
“The question is, when it was trying to harvest data, did it go into these other sites? So we’re not confirming that that occurred,” he said.

The incident comes after OpenAI and Anthropic, in separate submissions to a parliamentary inquiry this month, urged Australia to reconsider a ban on use of the country’s creative content to train their models.
“Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names,” OpenAI said in a statement.
It added that it “identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers … our models took actions we did not intend.”
The Australian breach is the latest of several recent incidents in which OpenAI has disclosed hacks or unauthorised activity involving its AI agents well after they occurred.
In some cases this was because the activity was only detected belatedly, and in others because the company initially elected not to disclose it.

A separate high-profile incident, a mid-July intrusion into open-source AI repository Hugging Face, was only detected about a week after it took place, according to timelines released by OpenAI and independent investigators.
This helped ignite global debate about the risks posed by increasingly powerful AI models.
Rivals Anthropic, Google’s Gemini, and Meta have also disclosed incidents of their agents accessing external systems.

Some of America’s top AI executives, including Altman, have called for a slowdown of industry development, citing, among other factors, the threat of devastating cyber attacks by out-of-control agents. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK losing up to £6.5bn a year in EU trade due to mismatched product rules
articles.summary:
IPPR finds failure to align testing standards has forced companies to abandon exporting to EU and is costing costing 0.18% of national income

The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU…

blocks.text: The UK is losing out on annual exports to the EU that could be worth as much as £6.5bn without a deal with Brussels that allows manufacturers to jettison duplicate product testing.

In the latest attempt to calculate the loss of trade with the EU after Brexit, the IPPR thinktank said many companies have given up selling goods to the EU or set up subsidiaries inside the trade bloc after successive governments failed to secure a mutual recognition agreement that would avoid the extra administration costs.

The thinktank estimated that the absence of such a deal may have cost UK exporters between £3.7bn and £6.5bn each year in lost revenue since the UK’s post-Brexit trading arrangements came into force in 2021.

It urged the government to reopen talks with the EU, saying that the loss of trade amounted to about 0.18% of annual national income, or about three times what the UK government expects to gain from its trade deal with Japan, Canada, Australia and Singapore, known as the CPTPP deal.

At this week’s Liberal Democrat conference, the party’s leader, Ed Davey, said that should the party take control at Westminster, he would begin talks to rejoin the EU single market and customs union.
He said the move would bring the UK into alignment with its largest trading partner, boost exports and kickstart growth.
Earlier this year, the Starmer administration pitched the creation of a single market for goods between the UK and EU to Brussels, but the proposal was rejected by EU officials.
EU officials said they wanted deeper cooperation with the UK, but this had to be in line with fundamental principles, including no cherrypicking of EU policies.

The IPPR said a mutual recognition agreement (MRA) based on “dynamic alignment” – where the UK keeps relevant product rules in step with the EU – would allow UK and EU authorities to recognise each others’ product assessments, reducing costs and uncertainty for exporters.
The estimated losses are concentrated in three industries:

items: Motor vehicle and part exports would have been between £2.48bn and £3.42bn higher each year.
Electronic exports could have been between £1.17bn and £1.67bn higher.
Pharmaceutical exports would have had an estimated annual uplift of between £740m and £820m.

blocks.text: after newsletter promotion

“The findings highlight the scale of trade missed out on as a result of post-Brexit regulatory barriers, providing one of the clearest opportunities to reduce friction in UK-EU relations,” the report said.

Joseph Sassoon, an economist at the IPPR and co-author of the report, said the report was the first attempt to find the cause of the loss of trade after Brexit by isolating its impact from other factors that could also have caused exports to decline.

He said researchers tested whether Covid-related disruption, changes in global supply chains, sanctions on Russia, energy market shocks or shifts in re-export patterns could be to blame for the decline.
“The estimated impact of not having an MRA remained large and statistically significant throughout,” he said.

articles.title: Elif Eralp: ‘Germany’s Zohran Mamdani’ who vows to be a mayor for all Berliners
articles.summary:
Die Linke candidate, a lawyer affected by her experiences as the child of political migrants from Turkey, poised to head Berlin coalition government

Elif Eralp launched her election bid last…

blocks.text: Elif Eralp launched her election bid last autumn with the blunt statement: “People like me are actually not supposed to become mayor in this country.” So the fact that the 45-year-old lawyer and daughter of political migrants from Turkey is on the verge of becoming Berlin’s next mayor and the capital’s first leader of Turkish origin is quite the moment in German politics.
After last weekend’s city state election, in which her far-left party, Die Linke, came first with more than a quarter of the votes, Eralp has become a household name.

The mood at Die Linke’s election celebrations on Sunday night was electric. Eralp, whose candidacy has helped propel the party from the doldrums to the brink of heading a coalition government in Berlin for the first time, was feted as a star.

blocks.caption: Eralp’s candidacy for Die Linke has helped propel the party from the doldrums and turned her into a household name. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: Some commentators suggested Germany was “having a [Zohran] Mamdani moment”, in reference to the democratic socialist mayor of New York. (One of his advisers was summoned to Berlin to help Eralp weeks before the poll. Her campaign was modelled on that of the veteran US senator Bernie Sanders.)

“In our city, love and justice won over hate … this signal goes out into the world,” Eralp said at her victory party, the “hate” a pointed reference to the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, which was celebrating coming first in another regional election. Even in liberal Berlin, the populist party made considerable gains.

It was Die Linke, however, that came out on top. With about 26% of the vote, the party not only outperformed the centre-left Social Democrats, whose presence has dominated Berlin politics for decades, and the Greens. It was also well ahead of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the conservative party of the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, which had previously held the mayoral position.
A lot is now at stake for Eralp, who has promised to be “a mayor for all Berliners”.

Eralp, who was chosen in particular by the young (47% of whom voted for her) and who mobilised thousands of otherwise non-voters thanks in part to intensive door-to-door campaigning and social media, generated most interest with her ambitious promise to take on corporate giants over unaffordable housing in the German capital. Once described as “poor but sexy” by a former mayor for its low cost of living, Berlin’s rents have soared in recent years.

In her nomination speech, the lawyer said: “I’m running so that our city becomes affordable again, so that real estate speculators don’t decide what happens to our city, but rather we do together.” She called sky-high rents a defining social issue, saying: “This city belongs to all of us, not to the speculators.”

Merz has led the charge against Eralp’s plans to expropriate more than 200,000 Berlin flats from their corporate landlords, saying her policy – decried by some as “socialism on speed” – would have “calamitous effects” on the economy. The chancellor has said he will push for laws to prevent her plans. Eralp has pledged to plough on.

blocks.caption: Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor and leader of the CDU, reacts to the state election results. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: It is not a given that Die Linke will take control of Berlin’s towering Rotes Rathaus, or red city hall, named after its red brick and not its association with leftwing politics. Eralp’s victory has been overshadowed by accusations that Die Linke has failed to tackle antisemitism within its own ranks as well as charges that the party has tolerated – and at worst courted – the support of criminal gangs.

The Social Democrats and the Greens, potential coalition partners, have said they need urgent clarification on these alleged affiliations before they agree to be associated with Die Linke. Die Linke’s leadership has repeatedly denied the accusations while vowing to clampdown on any antisemitism in its ranks. On Tuesday it announced that one of its Berlin MPs, who is alleged to have connections both to criminal gangs and a terrorist-related, pro-Hamas organisation, would “suspend his parliamentary duties until further notice”.

On Monday, Eralp sought to reassure critics. “Any form of glorification or trivialisation of violence or terror is completely out of the question,” she said. “I stand by that, and for me the promise of protection applies unequivocally to Jewish people just as it does to Muslims, Christians and all people in our city.”

blocks.caption: Eralp’s campaign was modelled on that of the veteran US senator Bernie Sanders. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty

blocks.text: Eralp has been keen to stress the ordinariness of her life. She lives with her husband and two children in a rental flat in her own constituency of Kreuzberg, in south-central Berlin, one of the city’s most diverse quarters and home to one of Germany’s liveliest Turkish communities. Her children attend a state school in her kiez, or neighbourhood, and she has kept her family away from the cameras “for their own safety”, she says. Much of her campaigning in the district was carried out in Turkish.

Unlike most Turkish migrants, Eralp’s parents did not come to Germany as Gastarbeiter, or guest workers, from Eastern Anatolia but were trade unionists and socialists from Istanbul who were imprisoned after a military coup for their political beliefs. Her mother, Hülya, a well-known feminist in Turkey, was only allowed out of jail because she was heavily pregnant with Eralp. She and Eralp’s father, Selçuk, a doctor, fled to Germany, where their daughter was born in Munich in 1981.

blocks.caption: Eralp poses for a selfie with a supporter. Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty

blocks.text: The family experienced a complicated asylum process, which Eralp has said helped shape her view of the world. “I’ve experienced a lot about what it means when authorities make decisions you don’t understand. I’ve also felt racism and discrimination first-hand, so my life story has a lot to do with where I’ve ended up now,” she has said. She recalls how her parents often put up asylum seekers in their home over many years, and the 15 years of struggle that her mother, a trainer for nurses, faced before her qualifications were recognised in Germany.

At the age of 10, Eralp founded a conservation club with friends in her parents’ garage, and later she went into the anti-nuclear movement. After studying law at the University of Hamburg, she moved to Berlin for two years of obligatory practical legal training, ending up working in the parliamentary group of Die Linke and later switching to the Berlin state parliament.
She said she was inspired to join Die Linke in 2017 in direct response to the entry of AfD, an anti-immigration party, into the Bundestag for the first time.

In 2019, with fellow members and supporters of Die Linke who had refugee and migrant backgrounds, she co-founded Links*kanax, an alliance that aimed to increase the visibility of the migrant-progressive voice within the party and beyond.

When she was 12, Eralp says, she wanted to become a human rights lawyer “to fight against all these injustices I’d seen”. Now, she says, “I’m doing what I set out to do, not in a courtroom, but in the political sphere”.

articles.title: The long-range drone war: Ukraine and Russia scramble for supremacy in the skies
articles.summary:
A conflict that began with tanks and then artillery is now pivoting around a new generation of drones focused on military, industrial, economic and civilian targets

Finally, in the dead of…
articles.byline: Dan Sabbagh in eastern Ukraine. With photographs by Julia Kochetova

blocks.text: Finally, in the dead of night, the threat above has passed. The rain has eased and the Ukrainian drones are ready, prepared by a ground crew shrouded in hard-to-detect green and red lights. A small succession of Ukrainian Fire Point FP-2 craft, miniature monoplanes with a 6-metre wingspan and more than 100kg of explosive, line up for an attack mission into occupied Luhansk, over 200 miles away.

The drone’s main piston engine is a familiar scooter’s buzz, but its launch booster is something else. The jet sound reverberates, almost painfully. A burst of fire lurches into the distance, the last of which signifies it is time for Ukraine’s 413 Raid drone regiment to pack and go.

blocks.caption: The launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied Luhansk

items: The launch of an FP-2 drone during the mission into occupied Luhansk

blocks.text: It is a scene that is now played out nightly by dozens of Ukrainian crews, reflecting a fast-changing conflict that began with tanks, then artillery, but is now pivoting beyond a first generation of drones. Death and destruction are delivered by new weapons in growing volumes, hundreds of miles beyond the frontline, and at targets that are military, industrial and economic but that affect civilians too.

But just as Ukraine has developed its drone and missile capability to almost match Russia’s – after its cities were subject at times to hundreds of drone strikes a day – Moscow has transformed its drone arsenal with a jet-powered revolution. The balance of power remains uncertain.

items: Pilots of the 413 Raid drone regiment preparing an FP-2 for launch

blocks.text: Raid is a specialist drone unit, created two years ago, and has been operating Ukrainian-designed and -built FP-2 attack drones since last autumn, according to Skipper, a former corporate IT worker with a master’s in computer science who is now one of its commanders. If, he says, there was only one crew that could run two missions a week when they started, today he says “we can do 10 times more, or even more”.

Speaking in a car as the rain pelts down, Skipper cautions there is “a flipside” when asked if long-distance wars are easier to fight because nobody has to be killed visibly. “They can do it as well,” he says – Raid’s crew are targets too. “Maybe you don’t see the enemy with your own eyes, but still it’s a very dangerous game,” he adds.

The FP-2 was only first publicly acknowledged by Ukraine last September. It is designed to attack hardened targets at a mid-range, to disrupt Russian logistics to the frontline. The success of Raid and others engaged in mid-strike bombing has helped grind the pace of the invaders’ advance to a near halt. Russia gained a modest 90 square kilometres of Ukraine in August, compared with 505 sq km a year earlier, and western officials estimate it is losing 6,000 more soldiers a month than it can recruit.

In Ukraine’s sprawling military, the specialist drone units of the Unmanned System Forces, including Raid regiment, work and overlap with army units working closer to the frontline and special forces. A major attack, such as the attack that disabled the Moscow refinery about 300 miles from the border on 20 September, involves several working at once.

A long-range attack could involve launching up to 300 drones, though the target is to be able to launch 1,000 a night, in what soldiers describe as an “orchestra”, where cheap drones identify an air corridor towards the final target.

blocks.caption: An employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images

items: An employee walks past a plume of smoke rising from a fire at the Russian e-commerce firm Wildberries’ logistics complex near the town of Podolsk, outside Moscow, on 16 August. Photograph: Tatyana Makeyeva/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The long-range, $75,000 FP-1, sister to the FP-2, has been used to repeatedly attack warehouses, refineries and other military-economic sites at a depth of 1,800 miles inside Russia, causing the country’s crude oil production to fall by 7.7% in a year, according to figures from the International Energy Agency, and interest rates to remain at 14%. “Both sides are getting better at translating deep strikes into economic effects,” says Sidharth Kaushal, of the Royal United Services Institute.

blocks.caption: A refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/Shutterstock

items: A refinery burning in Moscow after Ukrainian drones strikes, 21 September. Photograph: EyePress News/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Mission planning is rarely shown, but a short-range drone unit operating in the eastern Donetsk front – Unit 17, Special Operations Centre – is happy to show their war work from their dacha. Znakhar, 33, a software coder before the full Russian invasion, is one of a squad of English-speaking men in their early 30s. During the day, he clicks on fresh, static targets – artillery, electronic jamming systems – that have been added to a common system from western satellites or Ukrainian reconnaissance drones, studying their pictures for extra information.

blocks.caption: Pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike drone

items: Pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre, posing for a portrait next to a Sych mid-strike drone

blocks.caption: The temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikes

items: The temporary base of pilots of Unit 17, Special Operations Centre. Right: the ‘drop bombs’ Unit 17 used for middle strikes

blocks.text: At night, the crew use a $25,000 Sych drone, which looks like a large model aeroplane. If the rain holds off, they can fly two to six bombing runs, dozens of miles behind enemy lines. Znakhar, whose call sign means healer or herbalist, draws up an initial flight path in seconds with a few clicks on a map, then adjusts the route to avoid population centres, high ground and known interceptor drone launch sites. What’s changed recently? “More drones,” he says. “Russian drones.”

Colleagues such as Ananas, 30, head out at night, taking more precautions than they did when the unit started drone work two years ago, preparing launches underground where once they could work in a field. He studied architecture, then worked as a 3D artist in a video game studio. “I play a lot of video games,” he says, “so I’m good with a gamepad. It’s a big plus because now I’m a pilot.” It’s a narrowing of the gap between fiction and reality.

On the other side, Moscow always has ballistic and cruise missiles available, allowing it to bomb anywhere inside Ukraine since February 2022. It imported delta-winged Shahed drones from Iran in the war’s first year to boost its long-range attack numbers, and developed a family of cheap battlefield drones plus its own version of the Shahed. But since May there has been a notable set of upgrades, allowing Russian forces to strike Ukraine more effectively with fast, jet-engined drones, allied with a new ruthlessness of targeting.

blocks.caption: Firefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September

items: Firefighters working at the site of a Russian drone strike on Kyiv business centre on 23 September

blocks.text: “Russia never stops,” Serhii Beskrestnov, Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser, said during an interview in Kyiv punctuated by an air raid and explosions in the distance. The original Iranian delta wing Shahed (known by Russia as the Geran-2) has been redesigned and a jet engine added.

The new Geran-4, with more aerodynamic wings, flies at anywhere from 300km/h (186mph) to 550km/h, while the cigar-shaped Geran-5 is even faster, at closer to 600km/h. It is similar in speed to a new light cruise missile, the Banderol. The prediction is that Russia will make 36,000 jet Shaheds in 2027, a further 10,000 Banderols, plus a similar number of cheap cruise missiles, the Dan-T. All could be used to bomb Ukraine’s strained electricity, heating and water systems this winter.

The new weapons, whose Telefly engines are made in China, are faster than the Ukrainian interceptors, designed to stop the old piston-engined Shahed Geran-2s. Shahed interception rates, once over 90%, are down to 60% against Russia’s newer models, with predictable results.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village
The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in August

items: The aftermath of a Russian attack on ammunition storage in Myla village, Kyiv region, in August

blocks.text: A mix of jet- and traditional-engined drones made a rare morning attack into the centre of Kyiv on Wednesday, bombing a market near the central railway station and business centre, killing two people and injuring 41. At the end of August, a Geran-4 hit an ammunition dump at Myla, outside Kyiv, killing 38 and destroying homes nearby.

Another struck Ukraine’s SBU domestic intelligence agency in the centre of Kyiv, though it may have been controlled in its final phase by a Russian agent on the ground. Food supplies in Kyiv supermarkets are uneven after sustained attacks on warehouses in August; petrol stations in the capital were targeted in early September.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images

items: The aftermath of a Russian Geran-5-type jet-powered drone strike on an Ukrnafta petrol station in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv, 15 September. Photograph: Libkos/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ukrainian military propaganda is excellent at highlighting successful missions on social media, but the wider picture of the impact of its drone strikes on Russia is harder to discern. “This spring we had a really nice time and almost every night we could see one, two, three, four systems destroyed,” Skipper says. “Since June, July, they are just hiding.” Other Ukrainian military sources emphasise that Russia has improved its jamming capabilities, and cheap strike drones are simply not as accurate now.

In this long-distance war, civilian casualties are climbing. New UN figures show 2,222 killed in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, more than in all of 2025. In August, 368 were killed in Ukraine and a further 113 reported dead in Russia. Warehouses owned by Ukrainian supermarkets, its Nova Poshta postal service and e-commerce groups were hit at least 32 times. Wildberries and Ozon warehouses in Russia were bombed 17 times by Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Firefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attack

items: Firefighters at a warehouse in the Kyiv region after a Russian attack

blocks.text: The impact could be harder for Ukraine. “Russia has advantages that Ukraine does not,” says Kaushal. “A more diversified range of long-range weapons, more of an air defence network and more slack as a society, because its people have not faced so much pressure for so long.” Ukraine, meanwhile, faces economic pressure at a time when its war budget is overspent and needs to find £40bn more next year.

Yet, though war is escalating as the technology changes, neither side is close to defeat or a crisis. Tests will come if Russia tries to mobilise up to 300,000 men after parliamentary elections – and as Ukraine tries again to refinance and, most urgently, get through the winter.

Back in their soldiers’ dacha, Ananas and Znakhar wonder if the war will ever end. “Sometimes I catch this feeling,” Ananas admits, then Znakhar comes in: “We just need to hang on one more day than them.”

articles.title: Thank goodness for the storytellers — the ones who probe, question, irritate the powerful
articles.summary: In every community, village, town and region there are natural journalists: people who observe, record, analyze, remember, and challenge.

blocks.text: This is the year the world caught fire. Often literally — wildfires across Europe and America stopped even the most vocal of climate change skeptics. But also figuratively. We are reminded again how global supply chains are vulnerable to geopolitical shocks, how endless wars force whole communities into spaces they do not want to be and are not welcome.
And online, a torrent of AI-generated and distributed content pretends to try to make sense of it all but actually confuses and imperils us.

Thank goodness then for the storytellers. The journalists, the ones who probe, question, irritate the powerful. The ones who sit and listen with the grieving and try to understand those who are furious.

Technology turns up the volume of public discourse, but rarely gives us the information we need at the moment we need it. Journalists do. They turn people deluged with information into informed citizens, able to advocate for themselves and to push for change.
And they are everywhere. In every community, village, town and region there are natural journalists: people who observe, record, analyze, remember, and challenge.
They are the eyes and ears of our local media outfits, often in places where there’s no market significant enough to support the “classical” news operations.

They are the ones holding a camera and trying to stop their hands shaking as they film a glacier breaking away and sweeping away whole streets in Nepal. They are the ones who spot diggers rolling into a remote Kazakh town and wonder if the ramshackle gold mine that suddenly appeared is legal.
The journalists are also the ones who listen, who allow the voiceless to have a voice and help people tell the story of their lives.

And there are also the journalists who keep at that work long after the rest of the world has looked away. They are also the ones who stay to ask what happens next. How will homes be rebuilt after a catastrophe? Why are the glaciers melting? Who is behind the mining operations that are destroying a local landscape and why are regional authorities allowing them to operate without permits?

These storytellers and journalists need recognition and they need protection to keep doing their job. They need legal covers from the powerful who try to stop them from asking the difficult questions and uncovering the answers. They need a back up when fighting technology companies that profit from their work without paying for it.
Most importantly they need audiences, readers and communities that recognize and value the importance of what they do.

Our information ecosystems — the digital, audio visual and written messages we receive in our everyday lives — still need journalists to function properly. And crucially they need a plurality of journalists — the small, independent outlets to harness the energy of the streets, and the large, well-established newsrooms willing to take on the big fights.
This is a challenge for generations. Across the world young people are picking up cameras and phones to record their own stories and walk into public life with demands, questions, and ideas.

This is a huge opportunity for the new mobile-first outlets that carry their stories across social media, but it is also the chance for larger, more established newsrooms to win the trust of the younger audiences they have been searching for.

It matters to all of us. There can be no meaningful civil participation without facts, context, and questions. Anyone who wants to sow confusion and misery takes away information, silences those who ask questions, and denies people the right to know about the world around them. There is an easy way to fight back. Read the news, tell your story, be informed. Be heard. – Rappler.com
Meera Selva is CEO at Internews Europe. This opinion piece was commissioned as part of the World News Day campaign, an initiative to show the value of journalism.

articles.title: 40 Pinoy seafarers safe in Singapore Strait ship collision
articles.summary: On September 17, Panama-flagged bulk carrier First Margaux collided with a China-registered fishing vessel Lu Qing Yuan Yu.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 11:39am
This photo taken on April 21, 2026, shows vessels in the Singapore straits.
AFP / Roslan Rahman

MANILA, Philippines — Around 40 Filipino seafarers aboard the Panama-flagged bulk carrier First Margaux were identified and confirmed safe by the government following a collision with a Chinese fishing vessel in Singapore Strait.

Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) Secretary Han Leo Cacdac said on the sidelines of Philippine Maritime Convention 2026 on Thursday, September 23, that none of the identified Filipino crew members were hurt in the incident
“There have been no reports of any injury to Filipino seafarers onboard. However, at this stage, we are still gathering relevant information from the manning agency pa,” Cacdac said.
The migrant agency chief added that they are already coordinating with the families of the Filipino seafarers aboard the First Margaux.

The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said in a press release on Tuesday, September 22, that they are currently investigating the September 17 collision incident between First Margaux and a China-registered fishing vessel Lu Qing Yuan Yu.
“The fishing vessel took on water during the incident but remained afloat and stable, with the crew taking measures to manage the situation onboard,” MPA said.
Cacdac assured that appropriate assistance will be provided to affected seafarers.
Seafarers protection
Repatriation efforts continue for Filipino seafarers caught in conflict in the Strait of Hormuz and Black Sea, according to Cacdac.

According to DMW, a total of seven Filipino seafarers have been killed in the conflict-affected areas this year. Four of them died due to attacks while passing Hormuz, while three were killed in the Black Sea.

The Hormuz Strait remains a high-risk area for seafarers due to intensified tensions between Iran and United States-Israel, while deployment of Filipino seafarers in Black Sea has been banned due to the continued Ukraine-Russia conflict.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen waiting to hear U.S. President Donald Trump speak to the United Nations General Assembly at the UN headquarters on Tuesday. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada. In a lengthy New York Times interview, he declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called "extreme tail risk."
PM would not say in detail what that examination involved
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

In a lengthy New York Times interview published Wednesday, Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called "extreme tail risk."
Carney also spoke in the interview about Canada's plans to reduce its reliance on Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.
He also discussed Canada considering alternatives to buying American F-35 fighter jets.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state, and while he ruled out using military force to annex Canada in January 2025, he has said he would consider using "economic force" to get Canada to become part of the United States.

The New York Times report says Carney disclosed that he and Trump speak "frequently," even since trade talks collapsed last month, something the prime minister has said multiple times in recent weeks.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 9:39am
Satellite rendering shows Typhoon Storm Queenie (international name: Surigao) taken as of 7:30 a.m. of Sept. 14, 2026.
PAGASA via Facebook
MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Storm Surigae entered the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) early Thursday morning, state weather bureau PAGASA said.
The storm was assigned the local name Queenie after it entered PAR at around 7 a.m. Thursday, September 24.
Queenie is the 17th tropical cyclone to enter the PAR this year.
In its earlier forecast, PAGASA said Queenie was packing maximum sustained winds of 75 kilometers per hour near the center and gustiness of up to 90 kph.
The tropical storm was being monitored east of Northern Luzon before entering PAR.
PAGASA said it will issue its first tropical cyclone bulletin for Queenie at 11 a.m. Thursday.

articles.title: Germany sets out plan to phase out fossil fuels by 2045
articles.summary: Germany sets out a plan to phase out coal, oil and gas by 2045, reaffirming a climate strategy focused on electrification.

image.caption: Germany largely imports petroleum and natural gas to cover its domestic demand Image: Ina Fassbender/AFP

blocks.text: Germany has presented a roadmap to phase out fossil fuels by 2045.
Germany's Environment Minister Carsten Schneider told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that the plan "combines independence, affordability, and climate protection."

Europe's largest economy is now the third country to have provided a solid plan for the phaseout — to which nearly 200 countries committed at the 2023 COP28 climate conference in Dubai — following France and the Netherlands.
What did Berlin say about the fossil phaseout plan?
Schneider, of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said the decision was linked to the Iran war and its impact on fuel supplies worldwide.

"It is not just extreme weather events around the world that demonstrate how urgently we need to do more to protect the climate," he said. "If the situation in the Strait of Hormuz determines whether people can still afford their daily commute to work, that is not a good state of affairs."
Germany's chemical industry hit by high energy prices
He said he believed the 19-year deadline was feasible.
"Our roadmap is intended to set an international example. I am sure that many other countries will follow."
Schneider said that fossil fuels accounted for 65% of Germany's energy consumption in 2024.

The majority of that — 98% of its oil and 95% of its natural gas — was imported at a cost of €76 billion ($86.5 billion). The minister stressed that the figure has since risen sharply due to the Iran war.
How have environmental organizations reacted to the plan?
Several environmental organizations welcomed Berlin's plan, though some highlighted that it contradicted some recent government decisions.
"With this announcement, Germany is showing a sign of life in international climate policy," said Greenpeace energy expert Mira Jäger.
However, she noted that "at the same time, the federal government is subsidizing the oil industry, breaking the heating transition, and slowing down the expansion of renewables."
How does natural gas harm the environment?
Fentje Jacobsen, a climate policy advisor at the World Wide Fund for Nature, argued that the roadmap largely rehashed existing initiatives without adding "new ideas or additional ambitions."
"The current government is meanwhile planning to rely less on renewables and more on gas," she added.

Energy Minister Katherina Reiche of the conservative Christian Democrats has advocated building new gas-fired power plants, arguing that this would help stabilize the electricity grid and highlighting the intermittent nature of renewable sources such as wind and solar.

Reiche has also demanded preserving a larger role for combustion-engine vehicles using alternative fuels, a position that contradicts the phaseout plan, which foresees battery-electric cars accounting for 100% of new passenger car registrations by 2035.
Germany's car industry is a pillar of the country's economy, and the recent struggles it has faced have naturally been reflected in the broader economy.

articles.title: Cybersecurity agency clarifies extension granted only to Reddit, not Discord
articles.summary: The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center clarified that the extension granted to online platform Reddit does not cover Discord, which was also directed to establish a local presence in…

blocks.text: Headlines
September 24, 2026 | 9:22am
The logos of Reddit and Discord, two popular online platforms where users can interact, share content and join communities.
Reddit and Discord

MANILA, Philippines — The Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) clarified that the extension granted to online platform Reddit does not cover Discord, which was also directed to establish a local presence in the Philippines.

In a clarification issued Wednesday, September 23, the CICC said Reddit was granted an extension after its officials met with the agency online within the prescribed 24-hour period and discussed commitments to strengthen online child safety.

“Reddit was granted an extension after its officials met with CICC online within the prescribed 24-hour period and engaged with the agency on specific commitments that the Philippines urgently needs to strengthen online child safety,” the CICC said in a statement posted on Facebook.
The agency said Discord, meanwhile, separately reached out through a letter to express its willingness to discuss its existing teen safety measures.
However, the CICC said no extension has been granted to Discord pending direct discussions with the platform and concrete commitments on the agency’s requirements.

The clarification came a day after the CICC directed Discord and Reddit to establish offices and designate resident agents or local representatives in the Philippines within 24 hours of receiving its letters dated September 21.
The two platforms were also asked to submit written explanations of their existing safety and age verification measures.

The CICC had warned that failure or refusal to comply could prompt the agency, in coordination with appropriate authorities, to restrict their operations or prohibit access to the platforms in the Philippines.
Online safety concerns
The CICC's directive came after the September 18 shooting at Banga National High School in South Cotabato involving a 16-year-old Grade 9 student, in which three people died.

The agency said it is seeking the cooperation of Discord and Reddit in developing a framework addressing online sexual abuse and exploitation of children (OSAEC), child sexual abuse or exploitation materials (CSAEM) and nihilistic violent extremism (NVE).
It also asked the Department of Foreign Affairs to help arrange meetings with executives of Discord, Reddit and Meta to discuss online threats linked to violence and the exploitation of children.
The CICC said Philippine authorities are continuing to examine Discord over the presence of extremist communities on the platform, including groups associated with NVE.
These groups, the agency said, have been linked to the radicalization and recruitment of minors involved in recent school shooting incidents in the country.

The CICC previously said the directive was intended to ensure that online platforms are “reachable, accountable, and responsive” when activities on their services put Filipino children and communities at risk.
The agency apologized for any confusion caused by the clarification.
“We regret any confusion or misunderstanding that this may have caused,” the CICC said.
