articles.title: Synagogue shooting suspect's online username alluded to killing Jews weeks before attack, friend says
articles.summary: Sean Ward, the man who died after a shootout with police outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., was a former Armed Forces member who attempted to use an antisemitic handle to play an online video…
articles.byline: Eric Szeto, Christian Paas-Lang, Jordan Pearson, Megan McCleister

image.caption: Sean Ward, the suspect in a shooting at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday, used the name kitekiller in the game Once Human after his attempt to use a slur for Jewish people was censored, a CBC News visual investigation has found. Ward died in hospital Monday. (CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·CBC Investigates

Sean Ward, the man who died after a shootout with police outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., was a former Armed Forces member who attempted to use an antisemitic handle to play an online video game, according to a childhood friend and a CBC News visual investigation.
Sean Ward, who was a former Armed Forces member, died Monday after the weekend shooting in Belleville, Ont.
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 23, 2026 9:00 PM EDT | Last Updated: 29 minutes ago

The man who died following a Sunday shootout with police outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., alluded to killing Jewish people using a slur and railed against immigrants in interactions with a friend in the weeks leading up to the fatal attack, CBC News visual investigation team has learned.

According to a childhood friend CBC News spoke to, Sean Ward — a former member of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) — tried using a slur for Jewish people combined with the word "killer" as a username for an online game, but settled on "kitekiller" after it was censored. The friend was with Ward online on Sept. 2 while they waited to play the video game Once Human when Ward attempted to use the username.
"There was that one game we played … he tried to name himself the k--e killer, and it changed to 'kitekiller' because you can't obviously have that on there," said his friend.
The word is a deeply offensive term used against Jews.

items: Questions swirl as members of Belleville, Ont., synagogue return after shooting
Suspect in Belleville, Ont., shooting is dead, SIU says

blocks.text: CBC News is not naming the friend due to his fear that he will lose his job because of his association with the suspect.

Using text messages, online usernames and social media accounts, and an interview with the childhood friend, CBC News was able to put together a partial profile of Ward — a person who not only routinely engaged in antisemitic speech, but who more recently espoused anti-immigrant sentiments, blaming them for his lack of employment.
"He said he was depressed," said his friend, recounting a conversation with Ward earlier this month. "He was saying, 'F--k the immigrants', like … 'I can't find work.' "
"I just didn't think he would do anything to that extreme."

A spokesperson with the Special Investigations Unit, the civilian agency that investigates police conduct during shootings and other serious incidents in Ontario, said Ward, 29, died from injuries sustained during the exchange of gunfire outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville on Sunday night, where congregants gathered for Yom Kippur services.

items: Wife of wounded Belleville police officer says he faces 'long, difficult road'

blocks.text: According to the SIU, Ward is alleged to have fired at Belleville Police Const. Jeff Smith with a shotgun, then Smith and a second officer on scene returned fire, with dozens of shots exchanged.
Smith was injured in the confrontation.
Both were taken to hospital, where Ward died on Monday night.
So far, police have not released any information about the suspect's potential motivation for the attack.
'Don't do anything stupid'
The friend CBC spoke to said he noticed a change in Ward over a period of months this summer. His appearance changed, the friend said, noting Ward went from bulky to slim, with long, greasy hair.

"He just looked different. Felt different. I could feel a different vibe on him," the friend said. "Usually we talk more. So that's why I felt odd because, like, he wasn't shooting the shit like we usually did. Like, he was like, in his head kind of thing."
The friend said the last time he saw Ward in person was Sept. 2, roughly three weeks before the shooting.
"When he was leaving … I was like, 'Don't do anything stupid, bro.' I was like, 'I know times are tough, but don't do anything stupid.' "
Following news of the shooting Sunday, the friend messaged Ward.
"I immediately texted Sean," he said. "And the message never sent. So that kind of clicked to my brain that he probably did do it."
The friend said Ward always had his phone on. "Like always. He'd always answer pretty quick."

CAF confirmed Tuesday that Ward had served in the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry from 2017 to 2022. CAF did not comment on the reasons for Ward's release, but multiple people CBC News spoke to, including the friend, said Ward refused to be vaccinated.
The CAF vaccine policy required all members to be vaccinated against COVID-19 or face potential release. That requirement ended in October 2022.
A number of violent attacks have been directed against Jewish-owned businesses and places of worship in recent years, with several instances of firebombings or buildings being shot at.
Jewish advocacy group B'nai Brith Canada recorded more than 6,800 antisemitic incidents in 2025, the highest number it has recorded since 1982.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Eric Szeto is a journalist with CBC's visual investigations unit.

articles.title: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?
articles.summary: Meta has unveiled audio-only smart glasses, with some questioning whether it is a response to the backlash over privacy.

blocks.text: When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.
There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular, filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.

The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.

On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.
To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mark Zuckerberg - who wore a set at an event in California last year - predicts that smart glasses will replace mobile phones

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Mark Zuckerberg - who wore a set at an event in California last year - predicts that smart glasses will replace mobile phones

The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.
When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.
"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.
Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?

Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?
Music, maps, and washing cars
There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.

I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.

The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.
That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.

The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.
My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.

Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Left: Meta's demonstration of a user making a phone call, with an image of the person they're talking to displayed inside their glasses. Right: Zoe Kleinman wearing a set on her commute

blocks.text: Image source, Meta and BBC
Left: Meta's demonstration of a user making a phone call, with an image of the person they're talking to displayed inside their glasses. Right: Zoe Kleinman wearing a set on her commute

And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.
When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.

My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.

Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).

More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.
Calls for regulation
But still, anger over privacy has grown.

The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.

Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.
Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.
"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."
Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.
"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tech founder Liz Hunter is campaigning for tighter regulation of smart glasses

blocks.text: Tech founder Liz Hunter is campaigning for tighter regulation of smart glasses
A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine.

Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash".
The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however.

Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo.
Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone.
Step back or 'half step to the side'?

When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective".
So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable.

Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market.
Others are less sure it represents a real shift.

"It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it.
And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information.

"That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience."
He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release.

Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script).

Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'."

And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera."
And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera.
The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's.

Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate.
And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them - though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content.
"We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said.
He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras.
Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away".

He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says.
"We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products."

articles.title: In historic first, tropical turtles spotted nesting on California beaches
articles.summary:
What caused the turtles to begin nesting farther north than usual is the ‘million dollar question’

A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and…

blocks.text: A sea turtle crawled out of the surf in southern California last weekend around sunset and started laying eggs in the sand.

People on Huntington Beach who saw the female olive ridley sea turtle were shocked and excited. And they weren’t the only ones freaking out, said Justin Viezbicke, the California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (Noaa).
“This is the first documented case of a turtle nesting on the west coast,” Viezbicke said.

What made the sighting even more noteworthy is that two different olive ridley sea turtles were identified laying eggs on Orange county beaches in the last week, the first on Seal Beach and the second on Huntington Beach. It’s a pattern that has scientists questioning whether the nestings are a freak occurrence, or the beginnings of a more lasting trend.

While early news reports suggested that a single female turtle laid eggs on both California beaches, scientists further analyzed photographs of the turtles’ shell shape and barnacle patterns and determined that two separate olive ridley turtles had begun nesting on the US coast, Viezbicke said.
Olive ridley turtles typically lay their eggs on beaches much further to the south, in Mexico and Central America, Viezbicke said.

What caused the turtles to begin nesting further north than usual is the “million dollar question”, he said. Scientists are examining several different theories, including the environmental factor of warmer coastal waters, to other effects of El Niño, or whether the turtles “could have been blown off course by the recent hurricane”.
“There’s been a lot of activity in the Pacific Ocean,” Viezbicke said.

While it’s too soon to tell, it’s also possible that these first recorded US coastal nests could herald a broader northward shift in the olive ridley turtle’s nesting patterns, one driven by climate crisis and the warming ocean waters in the turtles’ native nesting areas, said Lance Adams, an aquarium veterinarian at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach.

The sex of the olive ridley turtle is determined by temperatures where the eggs hatch, and warmer temperatures produce more female turtles. “After about 87.8F, they’re almost all female,” Adams said. To achieve a balanced population, the sea turtles might need access to cooler nesting areas.
On the other hand, it’s hard to generalize from just two sightings, Adams said: “The turtles could be here by mistake.”

Because the nesting season is not over and individual olive ridley turtles typically lay multiple nests of eggs, “We might see additional sea turtles making beach crawls to nest in the next 30 to 90 days,” Adams said.
For protection, the new turtle nests have been surrounded by fencing. But there’s only so much local officials can do to protect the eggs, which typically take 45 to 60 days to hatch, Viezbicke said.

It’s not just the dangers from local predators, such as coyotes, or from interfering humans. New hurricane swells and high tides are expected as soon as Monday of next week, Viezbicke said – and there’s a risk of the extreme weather “washing away that part of the beach”.

Californians who spot sea turtles on a local beach should not interfere with them, and should keep at least 50 ft away, Adams, the aquarium veterinarian, advised. To advise authorities of a new turtle sighting, tell a lifeguard, or call Noaa’s marine animal stranding hotline, he recommended.

Getting close to the turtles’ fenced-off nesting spots is not a good idea, he said: “People won’t see anything.” If locals want to observe live sea turtles in action, they can visit rescued turtles on display in rehabilitation tanks at an aquarium.
Olive ridley sea turtles are one of the most abundant turtle species worldwide, but are protected under the US endangered species act.

Warmer ocean temperatures have led to sightings of all kinds of sea creatures that aren’t typically spotted on the California coast, he noted, including different shark species, rays, sea horses and the venomous yellow-bellied sea snake.
People should aim to adapt to shift in wildlife patterns, and, in general, keep their distance, Adams said, though new unexpected species present different potential risks.
“Turtles aren’t particularly dangerous to humans. They can bite. They can slap with their flippers. Someone could potentially get hurt, but probably not seriously,” he said.

articles.title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
articles.summary: With four measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania, health officials are hoping to get people on board with vaccines in private.

blocks.text: For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.

As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.
Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.

"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.
"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."

The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.

Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.
About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.

There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.

"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.
Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.
"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."

He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.

Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.

Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.
Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings.
"People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"
The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.
In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.

Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it.
"You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.
People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.

But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children.

"There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."
The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.

After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.
Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.

Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable.
"I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.
Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe.
"What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."

The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread.
"I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

articles.title: Residents eating garden weeds in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
articles.summary: The BBC has spoken to residents in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky who say they are being "constantly shelled".

blocks.text: Image source, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 and its people are now trapped
ByOlga Malchevska
Eastern Europe reporter
"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.
She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.
Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.
They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.
They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.
Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.
Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.
Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.

blocks.caption: Map showing the location of Oleshky and Radensk in Russian-occupied Ukraine. The location of the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson is to the north of Oleshky and Radensk, across a river.

blocks.text: It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023, flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.

Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.
Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.
Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.

blocks.text: Image source, Maxar Technologies Handout/EPA-EFE/REX/Shutterstock
Oleshky was flooded after the collapse of the Nova Kakhovka Dam in June 2023.
Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive.
"There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May.
"I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."
Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions

blocks.text: Image source, Ksenia Arkhipova
Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions
Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.

No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.
While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.

blocks.caption: Image caption, These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year

blocks.text: These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year
Warning: Distressing and graphic descriptions of dead bodies below.
Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult.
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan, external - about 24km to the east.
Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.
Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.
She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information.

"I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."
While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.

Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety.
"They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.
Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.
They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana.
Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.
Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".
Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".
That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish.
"This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.
"If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.

articles.title: Texas executes death-row prisoner over 2005 triple killing
articles.summary:
Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection, the sixth person to be executed by Texas officials this year

A man found guilty of fatally shooting three people during a 2005 attempted robbery…

blocks.text: A man found guilty of fatally shooting three people during a 2005 attempted robbery at a rural Texas home was executed Wednesday, a week after the other man convicted in the killings was put to death.

Ker’Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville. He is the sixth person executed so far this year in Texas, with three more people scheduled over the next two months.

A jury convicted Ramey of capital murder and sentenced him to death over the shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, in the home they shared in the small city of Edna, about 100 miles (160km) south-west of Houston.

Ramey and LeJames Norman believed there was cocaine in the house and hoped to steal it, according to court records. They found none and killed the three victims, who lived across the street from Norman.

blocks.caption: Ker-Sean Ramey in 2022. Photograph: Texas department of criminal justice/AP

blocks.text: Norman was put to death on 16 September, also in Huntsville. He had no last words, and no relatives or friends of the victims witnessed that execution.
The US supreme court rejected a final appeal from Ramey hours before Wednesday’s execution.

Ramey’s attorneys had argued that jurors never heard about how he suffered physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty. State prosecutors told the court the appeal was “meritless” and argued that evidence showed Ramey had “an escalating pattern of criminal behavior”.

Norman testified at Ramey’s trial nearly two years before being sentenced to death by a jury after pleading guilty to capital murder. He testified that he and Ramey shot the victims. Ramey’s attorneys blamed the shootings on Norman.
Ramey’s former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two pistols into a lake after the killings, and that he told her in detail about his involvement.
Lopez was shot four times, including in the back of the head; Peacock was shot twice in the head; and Roberts was shot five times in the chest, neck and head.

articles.title: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia
articles.summary: Campaigners hope the new words will lead to less body shaming and more sex positivity.

blocks.text: 'Make women feel seen': Why the Dutch have a new word for labia

blocks.caption: Image caption, Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word

blocks.text: Image source, Luciano Ölz
Shari Klein spoke at a recent march celebrating the new word
BySmitha Mundasad
Health reporter

Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.
Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".

European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.
"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".
"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.
'Sex positivity'
Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".
Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.
The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"

blocks.text: Signs used during a recent march in the Netherlands, the one on the left translates as "afterall there are no shame balls"

Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.
But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.

Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.
However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.
The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".
Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.
When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.
"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.
Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.
'Virginity membrane'
Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.

The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.
The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.
"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.
Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word

blocks.text: Supporters took to the streets in the Netherlands to celebrate and publicise the new word
In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".

She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria, external - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."
The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."
'Judgmental words'
Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.
"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"
New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.
Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.

One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.
"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen, external.
Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.
"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."
In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.
But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.
"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."

articles.title: Justin Bieber performs surprise acoustic gig in beleaguered Los Angeles park
articles.summary:
Small crowd enjoys singer’s free concert in MacArthur Park, which has often drawn headlines for less cheery reasons

With no announcement and little fanfare, Justin Bieber

blocks.text: With no announcement and little fanfare, Justin Bieber performed a free acoustic set on Monday at a Los Angeles park often in local headlines for less cheery reasons.

In videos that surfaced online, four musicians flanked the global phenom, who wore a plain T-shirt and shorts as he sang hits including Daisies and Yukon. The low-key affair with a small crowd stood in stark contrast to Bieber’s recent blockbuster World Cup and Coachella performances.
Some online users expressed surprise at the venue choice. A spokesperson for Bieber could not be immediately reached for comment about what spurred the show.

MacArthur Park, located west of downtown Los Angeles, is often described in ominous terms. The area has been plagued by gang activity and rampant drug use. Homeless encampments have also cropped up around the park in recent years.

blocks.caption: A jacaranda tree in MacArthur Park in May. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Earlier this year, federal authorities condemned the park as an “open-air drug market” after arresting several individuals who they accused of trafficking meth and fentanyl on to its grounds.
The park also became a flashpoint in the Los Angeles mayoral race, with mayor Karen Bass’s challengers using it as a benchmark for her progress on public safety.

In June, Bass disavowed crime in the park, saying the Los Angeles police were employing every resource to curtail illicit activity. Bass said the state and county had a role to play in the solution. “They must increase funding for treatment facilities and recovery services to stop the revolving door between jail and our parks,” she said.
Bieber’s performance comes after Los Angeles district attorney Nathan Hochman hosted a picnic at the park, following up on an earlier pledge to make the park family-friendly.
after newsletter promotion
“He’s definitely on the invite list for next year’s Labor Day weekend picnic!” Hochman wrote on X of Bieber.
“Bieber in MacArthur park. That’s progress,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli posted on X. “Amazing what can happen when criminals and drug dealers are removed from public spaces.”

articles.title: COA finds control, documentation deficiencies in OVP relief operations
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has cited the Office of the Vice President (OVP) over inconsistencies, deviations from guidelines, and missing or incomplete documentation in its relief operations…

blocks.text: The Commission on Audit (COA) has cited the Office of the Vice President (OVP) over inconsistencies, deviations from guidelines, and missing or incomplete documentation in its relief operations involving nearly P168 million in 2025.
In its 273-page report on the 2025 Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund (DRRMF), COA identified several deficiencies in the implementation of the OVP’s relief operations.

These included inconsistencies between situational reports, deviations from approved mission orders, the issuance of open-ended mission orders, and deficiencies in beneficiary and distribution records.
COA also noted missing or incomplete documents required to support the relief operations.

In its audit, COA identified inconsistencies between situational reports prepared by concerned agencies and local government units and those prepared by the OVP. The discrepancies involved relief operations covering welfare goods worth P19.67 million, including differences in the reported number of affected families.

State auditors also found that 24 relief operations involving P39.01 million worth of welfare goods deviated from approved Mission Orders without documented approval. The changes involved schedules, distribution locations, quantities of relief items and the amount of rice distributed.

The audit further found that eight Mission Orders covering P84.12 million in relief distributions did not specify target beneficiaries, instead directing the distribution of goods to affected or displaced families.
COA said this lack of defined beneficiary targets weakened the basis for determining the quantities of relief goods requested and distributed.

The audit team also identified deficiencies in beneficiary and distribution records, including uncertified master lists, discrepancies between Relief Distribution Sheets and master lists, incomplete beneficiary information, duplicate entries and unsigned distribution sheets.

In addition, COA said some relief operations used documentary requirements intended for the OVP's Relief for Indigents and Individuals in Crisis and Emergencies program despite being covered by the Disaster Operations Policy Manual.

The audit found that relief operations involving 33,980 beneficiaries and P25.27 million worth of welfare goods lacked complete pre-operation documents, including situational reports, Mission Orders and verified master lists.
In one case, a required Relief Distribution Sheet was unavailable after records were reportedly lost during Typhoon Kristine and was replaced with explanatory and certification documents.
COA said the deficiencies reduced assurance over the completeness, reliability and verifiability of relief distribution records and weakened controls over the OVP's relief operations.

The audit team recommended that the OVP strengthen its review procedures and ensure that operational adjustments, beneficiary lists and distribution records are properly documented, verified and authorized.
It also recommended that future Mission Orders clearly define the scope and coverage of relief operations whenever sufficient information is available during the planning stage.
Vice President Sara Duterte's spokesperson, Atty. Paolo Panelo, said that the OVP will release a statement about the matter after reviewing the COA notice.

"Kakatanggap ko lang ng mga request for comment tungkol diyan at nakikipag-ugnayan pa lang ako ngayong araw sa OVP, kung sino ang puwedeng sumagot dito. Maglalabas naman ng sagot o pahayag ang OVP kapag naaral na nila yung COA notice or letter," Panelo said in an interview on Unang Balita on Thursday.

(I have just received requests for comment regarding that, and I am currently coordinating with the OVP today to determine who can respond to this. The OVP will issue a response or statement once they have studied the COA notice or letter.)

"Kahapon, nung nag-usap kami ang sabi niya, laban tayo attorney. So, hindi siya natitinag, hindi siya magpapatalo sa mga latest development. Alam niyang tumitindig siya sa tama, so tuloy-tuloy lang ang laban," Panelo added.

(Yesterday, when we spoke, she said, 'Let's fight this, Attorney.' She remains undeterred and won't let the latest developments defeat her. She knows she is standing up for what is right, so the fight continues.) —LDF/ VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Indians are discovering the thrill of shopping without paying
articles.summary: Dopamine sites mimic shopping’s thrill without the spending, turning the ritual of consumption into a digital game.

blocks.text: Image source, Purvansh Parmar
FoodNeverComes calls itself a 'dopamine kitchen'
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.

You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.

Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.
"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site., external Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."

Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.
It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes

blocks.text: The site offers 22 fake kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes

FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.

The genre took off in South Korea, external and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop, external or Fakehaul, external, for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.
What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?

The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.
Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.

Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.
He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily need

blocks.text: Purvansh Parmar says he spent a lot of money on a work trip on food and treats he did not necessarily need
What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.

"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.

Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.
Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.

Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025

blocks.text: Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images
Swiggy, a popular food delivery site in India, alone handled roughly 2.5m consumer orders a day in FY2025

Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.
Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".

"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.
Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.
"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."

blocks.caption: Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway.

blocks.text: TripNeverLeaves lets users plan a holiday before sending them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway.

What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.
Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".
But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.
Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.
"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh Bachchan

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
A festive sale of of e-commerce site in India featuring Bollywood star Amitabh Bachchan
But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.

Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".
"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.

Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.
"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."
He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.

blocks.caption: Image caption, TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go'

blocks.text: TripNeverLeaves lists 260 places 'you won't go'
The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.

The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.
Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".

"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.
For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.
What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

articles.title: Tony Blair says Britain should work towards rejoining EU in next 10 years
articles.summary:
Andy Burnham under pressure to revisit Brexit as poll suggests pledge to rejoin could boost Labour’s electoral chances

Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony…

blocks.text: Britain should work towards rejoining the EU in the next decade, Tony Blair has said, adding to growing pressure on Andy Burnham to abandon Labour’s reluctance to revisit the 2016 referendum.
The former prime minister has urged Burnham to use his 10-year plan in November to put the country’s membership of the union back on the table, a decade after it voted to leave.
In a paper entitled A Path to Rejoining a Reformed Europe, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI) calls for the UK to accept free movement of people and make a financial contribution as the price of entry.
The intervention comes after Burnham declined to rule out promising to rejoin the EU in the next Labour manifesto, though it also threatens to reopen the deep rifts caused by the vote 10 years ago.

In a foreword to the paper, Blair argues: “Britain should signal an intention if the terms are right to enter into a structured formal relationship with Europe and initiate a process of negotiation where everything is on the table but nothing agreed until everything is agreed.”
TBI researchers say in the paper itself: “Over the next decade, Britain should work towards the ambition of rejoining a significantly reformed EU.”

blocks.caption: Tony Blair speaking at a Board of Peace conference in New York on Wednesday. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images

blocks.text: Blair is the latest in a series of Labour figures to back rejoining the EU. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, has called the Brexit vote a “catastrophic mistake” and said the party should aim to rejoin the bloc, while Burnham himself told the Guardian last year: “I hope in my lifetime I see this country rejoin the European Union.”

But Burnham has said he does not wish to pursue membership of the union in the near term. When asked by reporters this week if it could be in the next election manifesto, he said it was a question “for another day”.

Others are sceptical of the electoral wisdom of giving the appearance that the party wants to undo the result of the 2016 referendum, especially in areas of the country where Reform UK has made inroads in recent years.
Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, dismissed the idea earlier this year as she warned against “reopening the circular arguments that we ended up in as a country”.

However, pollsters suggest Labour could benefit electorally by promising to rejoin. A new megapoll conducted by YouGov on behalf of the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain suggests the party could more than double its seat total if it goes into the next election promising to rejoin.

The survey of more than 13,000 people, undertaken in June before Burnham became prime minister, found that a pledge to seek membership would help unite progressive voters behind Labour while doing nothing to boost Reform’s vote.
after newsletter promotion

The results suggested the move could take Labour from a projected 136 seats to 321 – though those totals will have changed since Burnham came to office, which has given the party a poll lead for the first time in months.

The TBI paper calls for Britain to try to accelerate European market reforms using possible re-entry as leverage. It argues that pro-reformers in Brussels would have a significant incentive to work with Britain on a project to make the EU more economically liberal and to reform its regulations on energy and technology.

It adds that Burnham should scrap the government’s red lines of not rejoining, not allowing free movement and not entering the single market or a customs union. The paper argues that the prime minister should replace them with a single promise only to sign up to rules and initiatives that prove of economic or strategic benefit to the UK.
TBI has advocated in recent years for the UK to slow down its push to achieve net zero carbon emissions and is a heavy backer of increased use of artificial intelligence in government.

Its policy positions have brought scrutiny on some of the institute’s most high-profile funders, who include the technology billionaire Larry Ellison, and its clients, which include the government of Saudi Arabia.

articles.title: Palace defends P58.5-B local fund against 'presidential pork' claim
articles.summary: Palace responds to Rep. Erice, who is threatening an Supreme Court challenge to the proposed P58.53-billion local fund.

blocks.text: September 24, 2026 | 7:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang defended the proposed P58.53-billion Local Government Support Fund for 2027 against a lawmaker's claim that it amounts to a "presidential pork barrel."

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro rejected Caloocan 2nd District Rep. Edgar Erice's characterization of the LGSF as a discretionary fund under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., saying releases to local governments are subject to requirements and evaluation.

Erice has questioned whether Congress is giving the executive too much discretion over which local governments receive funding and how much they get. He has said he plans to challenge the LGSF before the Supreme Court unless tighter allocation rules are imposed.
In response, Castro said Erice was free to seek relief from the courts but should first examine how LGSF releases are processed.

"Karapatan niya tumakbo kahit saang korte pero dapat siguraduhin lamang po niya na mayroong basehan. Dahil kung mabibigyan lamang siya or aaralin po niya ang proseso kung papaano naire-release ang LGSF sa mga LGU, malamang ay maliwanagan po siya," Castro said on Wednesday, September 2.
(It is his right to go to any court, but he should make sure that there is a basis. If he studies the process for releasing the LGSF to LGUs, he will probably understand it better.)

Under the government's proposed system, LGUs seeking financial assistance must submit requests directly to the Department of Budget and Management, with applications subject to eligibility requirements, evaluation, monitoring and audit.
The proposed P58.53-billion LGSF for 2027 covers financial assistance to LGUs, the Growth Equity Fund and the Barangay Development Program.
"Hindi po ibinibigay ang pondo basta-basta," Castro said. (The funds are not simply released without basis.)
Palace cites Robredo

Castro pointed to Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo's P500-million funding request for the rehabilitation and modernization of the Jesse M. Robredo Coliseum as an example of how local governments seek support from the national government.

"Ipagpaumanhin kung magagamit muli natin ang pangalan ni Mayor Leni Robredo dahil siya mismo ay nagpapatunay na mas maganda nga po na mas lumaki pa ang pondo na maitutulong sa ating mga local government units, dahil malaki po ang ginhawa na naidudulot nito sa mga constituents," Castro said.
(Apologies if we use Mayor Leni Robredo's name again, because she herself shows how increasing funds that can assist local government units can provide significant relief to their constituents.)
Marcos turned over a P500-million Special Allotment Release Order for the coliseum project in February.
Robredo has said the project originated from a request made in 2025 and was intended to improve the coliseum as a disaster-resilient facility.
Castro also invoked a Supreme Court ruling that upheld the constitutionality of an earlier LGSF appropriation.

In a 2019 ruling in Belgica v. Executive Secretary, the high court upheld the LGSF in the 2014 national budget, finding that it had a sufficiently identifiable purpose of providing financial assistance to local governments.
"Sinabi mismo ng Supreme Court na ang LGSF ay hindi po bawal at ito po ay nasa tamang paggamit para sa ating mga LGUs," Castro said.
(The Supreme Court itself said that the LGSF is not prohibited and may properly be used to support our LGUs.)
